American Popular Culture. The shared entertainment, values, and tastes of ordinary Americans, shaped by mass media and commercial forces. From silent film and jazz in the nineteen twenties through radio, television, and now digital media, popular culture has defined American identity, aspiration, and social norms.

It has democratized cultural experience, making entertainment and lifestyle accessible to the masses while reflecting and reinforcing American assumptions about success, gender, race, and consumption. Jazz, born from African-American communities in New Orleans, became synonymous with the nineteen twenties and defined an era's rebellious spirit and modernity.

Silent film from the eighteen nineties to nineteen twenties created a global entertainment medium, with American studios in Hollywood dominating production and export. Readers' Digest, founded in nineteen twenty-two, and The Saturday Evening Post became mass-circulation magazines defining middle-class American taste and values.

Radio emerged in the nineteen twenties and thirties as the dominant mass medium, carrying news, entertainment, and advertising directly into American homes. Television, introduced widely in the nineteen fifties, became the primary source of entertainment and information, with shows reflecting and shaping social assumptions about family, work, and relationships.

Hollywood studios developed the star system, making actors into idols and driving consumer culture through fandom and celebrity. Advertising became a dominant force, using psychology and mass media to create desire and define the good life through consumption. American popular culture has become a powerful export worldwide, spreading American values and lifestyle aspirations across the globe.
